title: SMTP Service Extensions
summary: Defines a framework for extending SMTP, by which a server tells a client which service extensions it supports. It introduced the EHLO greeting. It was a standards-track document, later replaced by RFC 2821.

plainLanguage.summary:
When a mail server starts a session, it now lists the extra features it supports, one per line. A client reads that list and knows what it may ask for.

The list uses short keywords. Some are standard and registered, and others start with the letter X and are private to whoever built the server.

questions: how do smtp service extensions work
what is the difference between helo and ehlo
subtitle: How a mail server announces its optional features, starting with the EHLO greeting.

tldr.problem: SMTP needed new features, and the RFC wanted them added in one consistent way instead of as separate, haphazard changes.
tldr.mechanism: A client opens with the new EHLO command, and the server answers with a multiline 250 reply listing the extension keywords it supports. A registry kept by the IANA defines the keywords, and MAIL FROM and RCPT TO may carry extra parameters.
tldr.outcome: RFC 1869 was an Internet Standard that obsoleted RFC 1651, and it has itself been obsoleted by RFC 2821.

today: RFC 1869 was an Internet Standard and it obsoleted RFC 1651. It has itself been obsoleted by RFC 2821, which consolidated the SMTP specification, and RFC 2821 was in turn replaced by RFC 5321. No later RFC has updated RFC 1869 itself.

sections.title: Why SMTP Needed a Way to Extend
sections.content:
For the purpose of service extensions, SMTP relays a mail object made of an envelope and a content. The envelope is sent as a series of SMTP protocol units and is straightforward: an originator address, to which error reports should be directed; a delivery mode, such as delivery to recipient mailboxes; and one or more recipient addresses. The content is sent in the SMTP DATA protocol unit and has two parts, the headers and the body. The headers form a collection of field and value pairs structured according to RFC 822, and the body, if structured, is defined according to MIME. The content is textual, expressed using the US ASCII repertoire, although extensions such as MIME may relax that for the body, while the content headers are always encoded in US ASCII.

SMTP is widely and robustly deployed, but some parts of the community wanted to extend the service. This memo defines a means by which an extended client and server can recognise each other and the server can tell the client which extensions it supports.

The RFC emphasises that no extension should be considered lightly. SMTP's strength comes primarily from its simplicity, and experience with many protocols shows that protocols with few options tend towards ubiquity while protocols with many options tend towards obscurity. Every extension, whatever its benefits, must be scrutinised for its implementation, deployment and interoperability costs, and in many cases the cost of extending SMTP will outweigh the benefit.

Given that, the framework has three parts: a new SMTP command, described in Section 4; a registry of SMTP service extensions, in Section 5; and additional parameters for the MAIL FROM and RCPT TO commands, in Section 6.
sections.plainLanguage:
Mail servers were already good at one job, and adding more features to them is risky. A protocol with many options tends to be used by fewer people.

So the RFC offers a single, tidy way to add features: one new greeting, one list of names, and a way to pass extra details with a command.

sections.title: The EHLO Command and Its Replies
sections.content:
A client that supports SMTP service extensions should start a session by issuing the EHLO command instead of HELO. The server then gives a successful response, a failure response or an error response. If the server supports no service extensions at all, it generates an error response.

The specification extends STD 10, RFC 821, without affecting existing services. Two changes are needed. The first is the first command: RFC 821 says the first command in a session must be HELO, and this is amended so a session may start with either EHLO or HELO. The second is the maximum command line length. Because MAIL FROM and RCPT TO may now carry parameters, the resulting lines can exceed the 512 character limit, and that limit is amended to apply only to command lines without parameters. Each specification defining new parameters must also state maximum parameter value lengths, so implementors know how much buffer space to allocate. The maximum command length an implementation with extensions must support is 512 plus the sum of the maximum parameter lengths of all the extensions it supports.

The syntax of the command is ehlo-cmd ::= "EHLO" SP domain CR LF. If successful, the server responds with code 250. On failure it responds with 550. On error it responds with one of 500, 501, 502, 504 or 421.

The command is issued instead of HELO and may be issued at any time HELO would be appropriate. If EHLO succeeds, a subsequent HELO or EHLO results in the server replying with code 503. A client must not cache anything returned by EHLO: it must issue EHLO at the start of each session when it needs to know about the extended facilities.

A successful response is normally a multiline reply, where each line holds a keyword and optionally one or more parameters. The first line carries the usual HELO chit-chat with the domain and an optional greeting, then one or more lines each beginning with a hyphen and a keyword, and a final line beginning with a space and a keyword. The keywords may be given in upper, lower or mixed case but must always be recognised and processed case-insensitively, which extends a practice begun in RFC 821.

If the server cannot list the extensions it supports it returns code 554, and the client should then issue either HELO or QUIT. If the server recognises EHLO but the command argument is unacceptable it returns 501. If it recognises but does not implement EHLO it returns 502. If it finds the SMTP service is no longer available, for instance because of an imminent system shutdown, it returns 421. After any error response the client should issue either HELO or QUIT. A server that conforms to RFC 821 but does not support these extensions will not recognise EHLO and will return code 500, staying in the same state; the client may then issue either HELO or QUIT.

The RFC also copes with servers that behave badly. Some SMTP servers are known to disconnect the channel on receipt of EHLO, either immediately or after sending a response, which violates RFC 821. For maximum interoperability a client using EHLO is advised to check for connection closure after sending EHLO, before or after the reply, and to decide whether the operation can be completed without extensions; if it can, a new connection can be opened and HELO used. Other servers will not accept HELO after EHLO has been sent and rejected, which can sometimes be worked around by sending an RSET after the failure response and then sending HELO, though many implementations answer the RSET with a failure code such as 503 Bad sequence of commands, which can safely be ignored.
sections.plainLanguage:
The client says EHLO instead of HELO. The server answers with a list of what it can do, and every reply has a number that says whether it worked.

Old servers that have never heard of EHLO answer with a number the client already knows how to handle, so the session can carry on the old way.

sections.title: The Registry of Extensions
sections.content:
The IANA maintains a registry of SMTP service extensions, and each registered extension has a corresponding EHLO keyword. Every extension registered with the IANA must be defined in an RFC, and that RFC must either be on the standards track or define an IESG-approved experimental protocol.

The definition has to include seven things: the textual name of the extension; the EHLO keyword value associated with it; the syntax and possible values of any parameters associated with that keyword; any additional SMTP verbs associated with the extension, which will usually but not necessarily be the same as the keyword; any new parameters the extension associates with the MAIL FROM or RCPT TO verbs; how support for the extension changes the behaviour of a client and a server; and the increment by which the extension increases the maximum length of MAIL FROM, RCPT TO or both, over the length specified in RFC 821.

A keyword that starts with an upper or lower case X refers to a local extension used through bilateral rather than standardised agreement, and X-prefixed keywords may not be used in a registered extension. Any keyword offered in an EHLO response that does not begin with X must correspond to a standard, standards-track or IESG-approved experimental extension registered with IANA, and a conforming server must not offer a non-X keyword that is not described by a registered extension. Additional verbs are bound by the same rules: verbs beginning with X are local extensions that may not be registered or standardised, and verbs not beginning with X must always be registered.

The initial registry holds the six SMTP commands that RFC 1123 defines as optional: Send as SEND, Send or Mail as SOML, Send and Mail as SAML, Expand as EXPN, Help as HELP and Turn as TURN. The mandatory commands, according to RFC 1123, are HELO, MAIL, RCPT, DATA, RSET, VRFY, NOOP and QUIT.
sections.plainLanguage:
Every public feature name has to be written down in a registry, and the document that defines it has to say how it changes the protocol, including how much longer the commands can become.

Names starting with X are private. Anything else has to be registered.

sections.title: Extra Parameters on MAIL FROM and RCPT TO
sections.content:
Several of the extensions planned for SMTP will want extra parameters on the MAIL FROM and RCPT TO commands. The syntax extends those commands with an optional list of parameters, each of which is a keyword and, optionally, a value separated by an equals sign. A keyword is one or more letters and digits, which may contain hyphens; a value is one or more characters other than the equals sign, the space and the control characters.

All parameter keywords must be registered as part of the same IANA registration process. This definition only provides the framework for future extension, and no extended MAIL FROM or RCPT TO parameters are defined by this RFC.

Two reply codes cover the failure cases. If the server does not recognise or cannot implement one or more of the parameters on a command, it returns code 555. If the server is temporarily unable to accommodate one or more of the parameters, and the definition of the specific parameter does not mandate a different code, it should return code 455. Errors specific to particular parameters and their values are to be specified in the parameter's own defining RFC.
sections.plainLanguage:
Two of the mail commands can carry extra details, such as options the client and server agreed on. Each extra detail has a registered name.

If the server does not understand one, it says so with a number the client can act on.

sections.title: Three Ways the Exchange Can Go
sections.content:
The RFC gives three example exchanges, all of them on TCP port 25.

In the first, the client connects and the server answers 220 dbc.mtview.ca.us SMTP service ready. The client sends EHLO ymir.claremont.edu and the server answers 250 dbc.mtview.ca.us says hello on a single line, with no keywords. That indicates the server implements only the SMTP commands that RFC 1123 defines as mandatory.

In the second, the same opening is followed by a multiline answer: 250-dbc.mtview.ca.us says hello, then 250-EXPN, 250-HELP, 250-8BITMIME, 250-XONE, and finally 250 XVRB. The last line begins with a space rather than a hyphen, which marks the end of the reply. This indicates that the server also implements the EXPN and HELP commands, one standard service extension, 8BITMIME, and two non-standard and unregistered service extensions, XONE and XVRB.

In the third, a server that does not support SMTP service extensions answers the same EHLO with 500 Command not recognized: EHLO. The 500 response indicates that the server does not implement the extensions in this RFC, and the client would normally send a HELO command and proceed as RFC 821 specifies.
sections.plainLanguage: Three short transcripts show the whole thing: a server that offers nothing extra, a server that offers several things, and an old server that has never heard of EHLO.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC does not discuss security issues, and it does not believe it raises any that are not already endemic in electronic mail and present in fully conforming implementations of RFC 821.

It does point out one thing. The EHLO reply announces the server's mail capabilities, but all the information provided by announcing the initial set of service extensions defined in this RFC can be readily deduced by selectively probing the verbs required to transport and deliver mail. The security implications of extensions described in other RFCs are to be dealt with in those RFCs.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC says it adds no new security problems, and notes that the list of features a server offers gives an attacker nothing new, because each feature can be tested by trying it.

viz.caption: THE EHLO SYNTAX AND A MULTILINE REPLY (RFC 1869)

data.title: EHLO and its reply
data.code:
ehlo-cmd ::= "EHLO" SP domain CR LF

ehlo-ok-rsp ::=      "250"    domain [ SP greeting ] CR LF
                / (    "250-"   domain [ SP greeting ] CR LF
                    *( "250-"      ehlo-line           CR LF )
                       "250"    SP ehlo-line           CR LF   )

ehlo-line    ::= ehlo-keyword *( SP ehlo-param )
ehlo-keyword ::= (ALPHA / DIGIT) *(ALPHA / DIGIT / "-")

S: 220 dbc.mtview.ca.us SMTP service ready
C: EHLO ymir.claremont.edu
S: 250-dbc.mtview.ca.us says hello
S: 250-EXPN
S: 250-HELP
S: 250-8BITMIME
S: 250-XONE
S: 250 XVRB

items.label: SUCCESS
items.desc: The extension list, normally over several lines.

items.label: FAILURE
items.desc: The server cannot list the extensions it supports.

items.label: COMMAND NOT RECOGNIZED
items.desc: A server without extensions answers this.

items.label: NOT IMPLEMENTED
items.desc: The server recognises EHLO but does not implement it.

items.label: SERVICE NOT AVAILABLE
items.desc: The service is closing, for instance for a shutdown.

items.label: BAD SEQUENCE
items.desc: A second HELO or EHLO after a successful EHLO.

items.label: PARAMETERS NOT RECOGNIZED
items.desc: A MAIL FROM or RCPT TO parameter is unknown.

items.label: PARAMETERS NOT ACCOMMODATED
items.desc: A MAIL FROM or RCPT TO parameter is temporarily unusable.
